text: About the Author John Keegan is the Defence Editor of the Daily Telegraph and Britain’s foremost military historian.
text_raw:
About the Author
John Keegan is the Defence Editor of the Daily Telegraph and
Britain’s foremost military historian.

text: The Reith Lecturer in 1998, he is the author of many bestselling books including The Face of Battle, Six Armies in Normandy, Battle at Sea, The Second World War, A History of Warfare (awarded the Duff Cooper Prize), Warpaths, The Battle for History, The First World War, and most recently, Intelligence in War.

Armies in Normandy, Battle at Sea, The Second World War, A History
of Warfare (awarded the Duff Cooper Prize), Warpaths, The Battle for
History, The First World War, and most recently, Intelligence in War.

text: For many years John Keegan was the Senior Lecturer in Military History at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, and he has been a Fellow of Princeton University and Delmas Distinguished Professor of History at Vassar.

text: INTRODUCTION Pre-Heroic Leadership This book is about generals, who they are, what they do, and how what they do affects the world in which men and women live.
text_raw:
INTRODUCTION
Pre-Heroic Leadership
This book is about generals, who they are, what they do, and how what they
do affects the world in which men and women live.

text: It might be expected to proceed by one or other method favoured by those who have approached the subject before: the ‘traits’ method or the ‘behaviour’ method.
text_raw:
It might be expected to
proceed by one or other method favoured by those who have approached
the subject before: the ‘traits’ method or the ‘behaviour’ method.

text: The first takes as its premise the assumption that those who exercise military authority will reveal under examination a certain set of common characteristics.
text_raw:
The first
takes as its premise the assumption that those who exercise military
authority will reveal under examination a certain set of common
characteristics.

text: The second attempts to identify patterns of behaviour which distinguish leader from follower. ‘Trait’ studies deal in the qualities of energy, decisiveness and self-confidence. ‘Behaviour’ studies explore roles; roles of encouragement, dissuasion and coercion.
text_raw:
The second attempts to identify patterns of behaviour which
distinguish leader from follower. ‘Trait’ studies deal in the qualities of
energy, decisiveness and self-confidence. ‘Behaviour’ studies explore roles;
roles of encouragement, dissuasion and coercion.

text: Both are the methods of social scientists and, as with all social science, condemn those who practise them to the agony of making universal and general what is stubbornly local and particular.
text_raw:
Both are the methods of social scientists and, as with all social science,
condemn those who practise them to the agony of making universal and
general what is stubbornly local and particular.

text: I am an historian, not a social scientist, and am therefore free to believe that the generalship of one age and place may not at all resemble that of another.
text_raw:
I am an historian, not a
social scientist, and am therefore free to believe that the generalship of one
age and place may not at all resemble that of another.

text: Not only am I free thus to believe;
text_raw:
Not only am I free
thus to believe;

text: I actually do so, and all the more certainly after thirty years’ practice of my trade.
text_raw:
I actually do so, and all the more certainly after thirty years’
practice of my trade.

text: Commonality of traits and behaviour I certainly see in commanders of all periods and places.
text_raw:
Commonality of traits and behaviour I certainly see in
commanders of all periods and places.

text: But even more strongly do I perceive that the warfare of any one society may differ so sharply from that of another that commonality of trait and behaviour in those who direct it is overlaid altogether in importance by differences in the purposes they serve and the functions they perform.
text_raw:
But even more strongly do I perceive
that the warfare of any one society may differ so sharply from that of
another that commonality of trait and behaviour in those who direct it is
overlaid altogether in importance by differences in the purposes they serve
and the functions they perform.

text: For the general – the word itself is pregnant with ambiguity – may be many things besides the commander of an army, though he will certainly be that.
text_raw:
For the general – the word itself is pregnant with ambiguity – may be
many things besides the commander of an army, though he will certainly be
that.

text: He may be king or priest:
text_raw: He may be king or priest:

text: Alexander the Great was both.
text_raw: Alexander the Great was both.

text: He may be diplomat: in their different ways Marlborough and Eisenhower excelled as much at conciliation as at strategy.
text_raw:
He may be
diplomat: in their different ways Marlborough and Eisenhower excelled as
much at conciliation as at strategy.

text: He may be thinker rather than doer:
text_raw: He may be thinker rather than doer:

text: Moltke the Elder’s qualities were intellectual rather than executive.
text_raw: Moltke the Elder’s qualities were intellectual rather than executive.

text: He may command by surrogate authority of a monarch, as Wellington did, or by endorsement of a democratic assembly, which gave Grant his powers.
text_raw:
He may
command by surrogate authority of a monarch, as Wellington did, or by
endorsement of a democratic assembly, which gave Grant his powers.

text: He may be owed obedience only for as long as his decisions bring victory, the uneasy lot of generals in the Boer free states.
text_raw:
He
may be owed obedience only for as long as his decisions bring victory, the
uneasy lot of generals in the Boer free states.

text: He may be demagogue- turned-tyrant, and yet sustain his military authority, as Hitler did almost until five minutes past midnight.
text_raw:
He may be demagogue-
turned-tyrant, and yet sustain his military authority, as Hitler did almost
until five minutes past midnight.

text: Generalship is, in short, much more than command of armies in the field.
text_raw:
Generalship is, in short, much more than command of armies in the
field.

text: For an army is, to resort to cliché, an expression of the society from which it issues.
text_raw:
For an army is, to resort to cliché, an expression of the society from
which it issues.

text: The purposes for which it fights and the way it does so will therefore be determined in large measure by what a society wants from a war and how far it expects its army to go in delivering that outcome.
text_raw:
The purposes for which it fights and the way it does so will
therefore be determined in large measure by what a society wants from a
war and how far it expects its army to go in delivering that outcome.

text: A general may, given strong character traits and effective behaviour, carry both society and army farther than they believed they wished to travel.
text_raw:
A
general may, given strong character traits and effective behaviour, carry
both society and army farther than they believed they wished to travel.

text: But he too, even if, like Alexander, he both rules and commands, will in the last resort act as a man of his time and place: when Alexander learnt in India that his army yearned for Greece more strongly than for new worlds to conquer, he managed an appearance of good grace and turned his steps homeward.
text_raw:
But
he too, even if, like Alexander, he both rules and commands, will in the last
resort act as a man of his time and place: when Alexander learnt in India
that his army yearned for Greece more strongly than for new worlds to
conquer, he managed an appearance of good grace and turned his steps
homeward.

text: In ignoring the particularity of leadership, social scientists have been encouraged by unlikely allies, the strategic theorists.
text_raw:
In ignoring the particularity of leadership, social scientists have been
encouraged by unlikely allies, the strategic theorists.

text: Social science conceives itself as a benign discipline, one of whose purposes is to rob strategy of point by reasoning the causes of struggle away.
text_raw:
Social science
conceives itself as a benign discipline, one of whose purposes is to rob
strategy of point by reasoning the causes of struggle away.

text: But strategic theorists are, in their way, social scientists also.
text_raw:
But strategic
theorists are, in their way, social scientists also.

text: For their aim – and the aim is a recent one, since strategic theory in its pure form was unknown before the eighteenth century – is to reduce the chaotic phenomena of warfare to a system of essentials sufficiently few for an ordered mind to bend to its purpose.
text_raw:
For their aim – and the aim
is a recent one, since strategic theory in its pure form was unknown before
the eighteenth century – is to reduce the chaotic phenomena of warfare to a
system of essentials sufficiently few for an ordered mind to bend to its
purpose.

text: The process of its development has been akin to that of economics.
text_raw: The process of its development has been akin to that of economics.

text: Just as modern economists have learnt to perceive that the aims of the mercantilists – who perceived trade as a form of piecemeal conquest – were misconceived, so too have modern strategists come to teach that the
text_raw:
Just as modern economists have learnt to perceive that the aims of the
mercantilists – who perceived trade as a form of piecemeal conquest – were
misconceived, so too have modern strategists come to teach that the

text: methods and aspirations of earlier practitioners were rooted in false perception.
text_raw:
methods and aspirations of earlier practitioners were rooted in false
perception.

text: Ironically, economics and strategy have moved in exactly contrary directions.
text_raw:
Ironically, economics and strategy have moved in exactly contrary
directions.

text: Modern economists preach moderation: all grow richer, they argue, when none seeks advantage.
text_raw:
Modern economists preach moderation: all grow richer, they
argue, when none seeks advantage.

text: Modern strategists teach exactly the opposite.
text_raw:
Modern strategists teach exactly the
opposite.

text: There is no place, they insist, for moderation in warfare, of the sort that seemed to suffuse the warfare of cabinets and kings.
text_raw:
There is no place, they insist, for moderation in warfare, of the
sort that seemed to suffuse the warfare of cabinets and kings.

text: Its only justification is victory, and victory is won by methods of extreme ruthlessness – decision, concentration, offensive action.
text_raw:
Its only
justification is victory, and victory is won by methods of extreme
ruthlessness – decision, concentration, offensive action.

text: These are ‘the principles of war’ which we owe to the greatest of the strategic theorists, Karl von Clausewitz, who began to publish at the beginning of the nineteenth century.
text_raw:
These are ‘the
principles of war’ which we owe to the greatest of the strategic theorists,
Karl von Clausewitz, who began to publish at the beginning of the
nineteenth century.

text: The chronology of strategic theory-making is of acute significance.
text_raw: The chronology of strategic theory-making is of acute significance.

text: Clausewitz, like Marx, is commonly portrayed as free-floating in time, simply a mind more powerful than any which had applied itself to its chosen subject before.
text_raw:
Clausewitz, like Marx, is commonly portrayed as free-floating in time,
simply a mind more powerful than any which had applied itself to its
chosen subject before.

text: Rarely is either subjected to the rigour of contextualization.
text_raw:
Rarely is either subjected to the rigour of
contextualization.

text: Yet context, when theories as powerful as theirs are at stake, is all.
text_raw:
Yet context, when theories as powerful as theirs are at
stake, is all.

text: Marx was able to argue for the primacy of ownership of the means of production as a determinant of social relationships largely because, at the time when he wrote, finance and investment overshadowed all other forces in society, and the military class – exhausted by the Napoleonic wars and dispirited by the defeat of its interests in Russia in 1825 and in France in 1830 – was at an unnaturally low ebb of self- confidence.
text_raw:
Marx was able to argue for the primacy of ownership of the
means of production as a determinant of social relationships largely
because, at the time when he wrote, finance and investment overshadowed
all other forces in society, and the military class – exhausted by the
Napoleonic wars and dispirited by the defeat of its interests in Russia in
1825 and in France in 1830 – was at an unnaturally low ebb of self-
confidence.

text: Yet military power, represented in its crudest form by the robber-baron principle, can, of course, at any time it chooses, make fools of the financier and investor, as the history of investment in unstable areas of the world makes unarguably evident.
text_raw:
Yet military power, represented in its crudest form by the
robber-baron principle, can, of course, at any time it chooses, make fools of
the financier and investor, as the history of investment in unstable areas of
the world makes unarguably evident.

text: It can equally make fools of revolutionary leaders who put their trust in the force of ‘historical’ laws.
text_raw:
It can equally make fools of
revolutionary leaders who put their trust in the force of ‘historical’ laws.

text: Marx, in his heart, recognized both truths, feared more than any other the temperament – and the military class is ultimately self-choosing by temperament rather than material interest – that will seize arms simply for the pleasure that blood-letting gives, and constantly urged the politically conscious to learn the habits and discipline of the military class as the merest means of defending and furthering the revolution.
text_raw:
Marx, in his heart, recognized both truths, feared more than any other the
temperament – and the military class is ultimately self-choosing by
temperament rather than material interest – that will seize arms simply for
the pleasure that blood-letting gives, and constantly urged the politically
conscious to learn the habits and discipline of the military class as the
merest means of defending and furthering the revolution.

text: Clausewitz also belongs in context, though he is rarely put there.
text_raw: Clausewitz also belongs in context, though he is rarely put there.

text: His famous ‘principles of war’ – written originally as a school text for the
text_raw:
His
famous ‘principles of war’ – written originally as a school text for the

text: Prussian Crown Prince – are, in a sense, words to the unwise.
text_raw: Prussian Crown Prince – are, in a sense, words to the unwise.

text: It is inconceivable that Alexander or Caesar or Frederick the Great or even Wellington should have needed to be reminded that a general should husband his resources and expend them only for good purpose – which is what the principles of ‘decision’, ‘concentration’ and ‘offensive action’ counsel.
text_raw:
It is
inconceivable that Alexander or Caesar or Frederick the Great or even
Wellington should have needed to be reminded that a general should
husband his resources and expend them only for good purpose – which is
what the principles of ‘decision’, ‘concentration’ and ‘offensive action’
counsel.

text: It is even less conceivable that any should have needed reminding, from Clausewitz’s later work, that ‘war is the continuation of policy by other means’.
text_raw:
It is even less conceivable that any should have needed reminding,
from Clausewitz’s later work, that ‘war is the continuation of policy by
other means’.

text: Alexander, Caesar, Frederick, even Wellington – who had sat as a member of parliament and minister – inhaled war and politics in the same breath.
text_raw:
Alexander, Caesar, Frederick, even Wellington – who had sat
as a member of parliament and minister – inhaled war and politics in the
same breath.

text: All accepted without conscious reflection the interrelationship of force and persuasion; all understood the limits to which the exercise of force may be usefully pushed; all lived with the reality that there is only so much moral sacrifice to be extracted from peoples, only so much material sacrifice from their economic lives.
text_raw:
All accepted without conscious reflection the interrelationship
of force and persuasion; all understood the limits to which the exercise of
force may be usefully pushed; all lived with the reality that there is only so
much moral sacrifice to be extracted from peoples, only so much material
sacrifice from their economic lives.

text: The great texts of strategic theory that began to appear at the beginning of the nineteenth century, of which Clausewitz’s On War is incomparably the most incisive, as well as the most influential, must therefore be seen as products of their time and place.
text_raw:
The great texts of strategic theory that began to appear at the beginning
of the nineteenth century, of which Clausewitz’s On War is incomparably
the most incisive, as well as the most influential, must therefore be seen as
products of their time and place.

text: Clausewitz is often called ‘the interpreter of Napoleon’.
text_raw:
Clausewitz is often called ‘the interpreter
of Napoleon’.

text: But that description misleads because it is entirely circular:
text_raw: But that description misleads because it is entirely circular:

text: Napoleon, though achieving power rather than being born or thrust into it, both ruled and commanded, and in almost exactly the same way and for the same purposes as Alexander had done.
text_raw:
Napoleon, though achieving power rather than being born or thrust into it,
both ruled and commanded, and in almost exactly the same way and for the
same purposes as Alexander had done.

text: He, too, knew that war is an extension of policy by other means and his emperorship was a sustained exercise in that duality.
text_raw:
He, too, knew that war is an
extension of policy by other means and his emperorship was a sustained
exercise in that duality.

text: Clausewitz, who might as well be characterized as ‘the interpreter of Alexander’ or of Caesar, Wallenstein, Frederick the Great or any other statesman-general, was clearly not writing for his or for their like.
text_raw:
Clausewitz, who might as well be characterized as
‘the interpreter of Alexander’ or of Caesar, Wallenstein, Frederick the Great
or any other statesman-general, was clearly not writing for his or for their
like.

text: On the contrary: he was writing for a new class of warrior, whose upbringing and way of life distanced its members from the realities of politics by deliberate purpose.
text_raw:
On the contrary: he was writing for a new class of warrior, whose
upbringing and way of life distanced its members from the realities of
politics by deliberate purpose.

text: This class was the product of a division of labour in societies that were rapidly complexifying.
text_raw:
This class was the product of a division of labour in societies that were
rapidly complexifying.

text: Europe, almost until the end of the ancien régime, remained a society in which the ruling class was also a military class.
text_raw:
Europe, almost until the end of the ancien régime,
remained a society in which the ruling class was also a military class.

text: The sword, accoutrement de rigueur of anyone pretending to the title of gentleman, was the outward symbol of that identification.
text_raw:
The
sword, accoutrement de rigueur of anyone pretending to the title of
gentleman, was the outward symbol of that identification.

text: But the growing wealth of ancien régime states produced classes – mercantile, legal, academic – that would not tolerate their exclusion from politics simply
text_raw:
But the growing
wealth of ancien régime states produced classes – mercantile, legal,
academic – that would not tolerate their exclusion from politics simply

text: because of their swordless status.
text_raw: because of their swordless status.

text: The Revolution was indeed, in one of its aspects, a revolt by the swordless against the swordbearers, and its success in that respect was unmistakable.
text_raw:
The Revolution was indeed, in one of its
aspects, a revolt by the swordless against the swordbearers, and its success
in that respect was unmistakable.

text: Power did pass, as a result of the events of 1789, from those who held wealth as a result of ancestral feats of arms to those who produced, extracted, manipulated or lent it.
text_raw:
Power did pass, as a result of the events of
1789, from those who held wealth as a result of ancestral feats of arms to
those who produced, extracted, manipulated or lent it.

text: In that strict but narrow sense, Marx’s observation was an exact one.
text_raw:
In that strict but
narrow sense, Marx’s observation was an exact one.

text: But the separation of the military from the ruling class and the diminution of its influence did not entail its extinction.
text_raw:
But the separation of
the military from the ruling class and the diminution of its influence did not
entail its extinction.

text: On the contrary: military class merely ramified, and in two contrary directions.
text_raw:
On the contrary: military class merely ramified, and in

text: After the Granicus, he ‘buried [the Macedonian dead] with their arms and other accoutrements; to their parents and children he gave remission of local taxes and of all other personal taxes and property taxes … He buried also the Persian commanders and the mercenary Greeks who fell in the ranks of the foe’ (the common Persian soldiery may have been too numerous to honour properly); after Issus, ‘he gathered the dead together and gave them a splendid military funeral, the whole army marshalled in their finest battle array’; and, certainly after the Granicus and probably also after his other battles, he raised memorials to the fallen and sent trophies taken from the enemy home ‘to be hung in the temples to Athena [with] this inscription attached: “Alexander son of Philip and the Greeks (except the Spartans) [send] these spoils from the Persians in Asia”.’ Ceremony and Theatre To send spoils from the Persian War to Athens, greatest of the Greek states but also Macedonia’s least certain ally in the Hellenic League, was a calculated stroke of public relations; to associate his Greek followers with the Macedonians whom he proclaimed himself to personify – ‘Alexander son of Philip and the Greeks’ was an epitome of his army – but specifically to exclude the Spartans was a breathtakingly arrogant rescripting of the course of recent Greek history.

Ceremony and Theatre
To send spoils from the Persian War to Athens, greatest of the Greek states
but also Macedonia’s least certain ally in the Hellenic League, was a
calculated stroke of public relations; to associate his Greek followers with
the Macedonians whom he proclaimed himself to personify – ‘Alexander
son of Philip and the Greeks’ was an epitome of his army – but specifically
to exclude the Spartans was a breathtakingly arrogant rescripting of the
course of recent Greek history.

Hitler’s Soldiers
The essence of Hitler’s achievement of dominance over the German army
may be briefly stated: finding it humbled and diminished, he gave it back its
strength and so its pride, but he took from it in compensation, though in
scarcely perceptible instalments, its independence and autonomy and so
eventually its dignity and conscience.
